AAPP-17-001: Flynn classifies architectures by instruction and data streams: **SISD** executes one instruction stream on one data stream (a conventional sequential core); **SIMD** applies one instruction to multiple data elements (CPU vector units); **MISD** applies multiple instruction streams to the same data stream (rare; specialized redundant processing is a possible interpretation); **MIMD** executes independent instruction streams on different data (multicore CPUs and clusters). GPUs expose SIMT, closely related to SIMD within a warp, while independently scheduled groups provide additional parallelism.
AAPP-17-002: Mixing models is possible and often useful. For example, MPI distributes a simulation across cluster nodes, OpenMP uses the cores within each node, and CUDA offloads suitable kernels to GPUs. The relevant costs are coordination, data movement, oversubscription and programming complexity; increased binary complexity is not a general reason to reject hybrid programming. Match each model to the hardware level and give each level a clear responsibility.

AAPP-17-003: Yes. AAPP-17-004: False. Threads share the process address space and usually its I/O resources, so concurrent output can interleave and concurrent operations can require synchronization. Even when an individual library call is internally thread-safe, a sequence of calls is not automatically one atomic record, and output order is unspecified. Use a lock around a complete logical output operation or collect results and print them in a controlled order.
AAPP-17-006: Threads within a process share its address space and resources; each has its own execution state and stack. They communicate through shared data and need synchronization to prevent races. Separate processes normally have separate address spaces and exchange data explicitly, for example with MPI messages. Thread models naturally fit a shared-memory node; message passing also spans distributed-memory machines. Process-based communication can run within one node too, and hybrid programs combine the two.
AAPP-17-007: Manual parallelization can exploit domain knowledge that a compiler cannot safely infer: independence despite pointer aliasing, suitable data decomposition, algorithm changes, acceptable reductions, granularity and placement. Automatic parallelization remains useful where independence can be established, particularly regular loops and vectorization. Manual parallelization is therefore often needed for larger structural changes, rather than being universally preferable for every loop.
AAPP-17-008: True. Exposing many concurrent operations is only one requirement. A useful algorithm must also keep total work close to the best sequential algorithm, limit communication and synchronization, provide enough work per task, balance the load and use memory efficiently. Creating millions of tiny tasks can expose more parallelism yet run slower because management overhead dominates. Judge both work/span and the costs of mapping the computation onto the target hardware.

AAPP-17-012:
**PCAM** means **Partitioning, Communication, Agglomeration, Mapping**. First divide computation/data into fine-grained tasks; then identify their required communication and dependencies. Combine tasks to obtain useful granularity and locality, and finally assign them to processors to balance the load and control communication. These stages guide exploration and may be revisited as costs become clearer.

**Reference:** [Foster, PCAM methodology](https://www.mcs.anl.gov/~itf/dbpp/text/node15.html).

It reduces task-management and communication overhead and improves locality, while retaining enough tasks to balance the processors. For example, combine individual image pixels into tiles. Excessive agglomeration reduces concurrency, so the aim is an efficient granularity rather than the fewest possible tasks.

**Reference:** [Foster, PCAM methodology](https://www.mcs.anl.gov/~itf/dbpp/text/node15.html).

It is useful when an operation consumes most fields of each object. **SoA**, structure of arrays, stores one array per field, for example `x[i], y[i], z[i]`. It gives contiguous access when processing one field across many objects and often helps SIMD vectorization and GPU memory coalescing. The best layout depends on the actual access pattern; blocked mixtures are also possible.

AAPP-19-001:
Map applies a function independently to each element: $y_i=f(x_i)$. Assume independent outputs and no conflicting shared side effects. For constant-cost $f$, PRAM depth is $O(1)$ with $n$ processors and work is $\Theta(n)$; with $p$ processors time is $\Theta(\lceil n/p\rceil)$ in the ideal model. Example: square each array element.

```c
#pragma omp parallel for
for (int i=0; i<n; ++i) y[i] = f(x[i]);
```

Two successive maps can fuse to `y[i]=g(f(x[i]))`, eliminating a temporary array and an extra traversal, provided intermediate values are not otherwise needed.

AAPP-19-019: Gather is output-driven: `out[i]=in[index[i]]`, so each output selects an input and repeated indices cause only shared reads. Scatter is input-driven: `out[index[i]]=in[i]`, so each input chooses its destination and repeated indices cause write collisions. AAPP-19-008:
Scatter uses one destination index per input:

```text
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:

```

Assume valid indices, disjoint input/output storage, and specify how collisions are handled. With distinct destinations, EREW PRAM depth is $O(1)$ using $n$ processors and work is $\Theta(n)$. AAPP-19-009:
Pack is stable filtering: retain exactly the elements whose Boolean flags are 1, in original order. Compute each selected element's destination with an exclusive prefix sum, then scatter:

```text
b[i] = predicate(x[i]) ? 1 : 0          // parallel map
s = exclusive_scan(b, +, 0)
K = (n == 0) ? 0 : s[n-1] + b[n-1]
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:
    if b[i] == 1: out[s[i]] = x[i]
```

Selected destinations are unique, so there are no write collisions. With constant-cost predicates and a work-efficient scan, depth is $\Theta(\log n)$ and work is $\Theta(n)$ on EREW PRAM. Example: `[a,b,c,d]` with flags `[1,0,1,0]` produces `[a,c]`.

Unpack places a packed sequence into positions selected by a known mask, supplying a specified default at unselected positions. It requires the mask (or equivalent position information); it cannot recover discarded original values from the packed sequence alone.

```text
s = exclusive_scan(mask, +, 0)
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:
    out[i] = mask[i] ? packed[s[i]] : default_value
```

AAPP-19-011:
Split stably partitions elements into two groups according to a Boolean predicate, retaining their relative order within each group. Let group 1 precede group 0:

```text
b[i] = predicate(x[i]) ? 1 : 0
s = exclusive_scan(b, +, 0)
K = (n == 0) ? 0 : s[n-1] + b[n-1]
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:
    pos = b[i] ? s[i] : K + (i - s[i])
    out[pos] = x[i]
```

The two destination ranges are disjoint and each element has a unique position. This is two complementary stable packs, implemented with one scan and one scatter. With a work-efficient scan it takes $\Theta(n)$ work and $\Theta(\log n)$ depth on EREW PRAM. Bin generalizes classification to multiple buckets rather than just two; bucket sizes/offsets and collision-free positions must then be computed.

AAPP-19-010: A stencil computes each output from a fixed neighborhood of input values, for example a 2D five-point average. Define boundary behavior and use separate input/output buffers, or otherwise preserve which time step each read sees. With a constant-size neighborhood and $n$ output cells, one step has $\Theta(n)$ work and $O(1)$ depth with $n$ processors on CREW PRAM. Overlapping neighborhoods create concurrent reads, so EREW needs replication or an appropriate schedule. Multiple time steps require dependencies between steps, often implemented using double buffering and barriers or tiled wavefronts.

AAPP-19-017:
Pipeline parallelism divides each item into ordered stages, while overlapping different items across stages. Example: read frame $k+1$, filter frame $k$, encode frame $k-1$. Use Pthreads stage workers with synchronized bounded queues, or OpenMP tasks with producer/consumer `depend` clauses and storage that remains alive until completion. OpenMP's basic execution model is fork-join; a pipeline is an additional pattern that must be expressed explicitly. Good throughput requires enough items, sufficiently large stages and a balanced bottleneck stage, with communication costs controlled. If stage times are $t_1,\ldots,t_s$, ideal steady-state time per item cannot beat $\max t_i$; startup/drain still cost roughly $\sum t_i$.

**Reference:** [OpenMP 5.2 specification](https://www.openmp.org/wp-content/uploads/OpenMP-API-Specification-5-2.pdf).

AAPP-19-064:
Pipeline parallelism divides each item into ordered stages, while overlapping different items across stages. Example: read frame $k+1$, filter frame $k$, encode frame $k-1$. Use Pthreads stage workers with synchronized bounded queues, or OpenMP tasks with producer/consumer `depend` clauses and storage that remains alive until completion. OpenMP's basic execution model is fork-join; a pipeline is an additional pattern that must be expressed explicitly. Good throughput requires enough items, sufficiently large stages and a balanced bottleneck stage, with communication costs controlled. If stage times are $t_1,\ldots,t_s$, ideal steady-state time per item cannot beat $\max t_i$; startup/drain still cost roughly $\sum t_i$.

**Reference:** [OpenMP 5.2 specification](https://www.openmp.org/wp-content/uploads/OpenMP-API-Specification-5-2.pdf).
AAPP-19-025: Scan produces every prefix of a sequence under an associative operator. Inclusive scan is $y_i=x_0\circ\cdots\circ x_i$; exclusive scan is $y_0=e$ and $y_i=x_0\circ\cdots\circ x_{i-1}$, where $e$ is the identity. For `[3,1,4]`, addition gives inclusive `[3,4,8]` and exclusive `[0,3,4]`. A work-efficient tree up-sweep/down-sweep uses $\Theta(n)$ work and $\Theta(\log n)$ depth on EREW PRAM; simple recursive doubling instead uses $\Theta(n\log n)$ work. Preserve operand order for noncommutative operators. Scan computes positions for Pack, Unpack, Split and Unsplit.

AAPP-19-002: The **workpile** pattern maintains a shared collection of pending tasks, which workers repeatedly remove and execute; tasks may generate additional tasks. It suits irregular searches and graph/tree exploration where work and task count are not known in advance. A fixed Pthreads pool can use a mutex-protected queue and condition variables; OpenMP tasks provide a higher-level implementation. Protect queue operations, balance granularity, and detect termination using both pending and active tasks: an empty queue alone does not mean active workers will create no more work.
AAPP-19-003: **Fork-join** starts concurrent branches and waits for their completion before continuing. It fits independent subproblems in divide-and-conquer, such as recursively sorting both halves. OpenMP uses `parallel` for a team and tasks within a `single` region to create recursive work, followed by `taskwait` or a `taskgroup`; Pthreads uses `pthread_create` and `pthread_join`. A task pool avoids creating an operating-system thread at every recursive call. Choose a sequential cutoff for small subproblems.
AAPP-19-004: Yes, the two recursive subproblems after partitioning are independent and map naturally to tasks, but efficient scaling needs more than spawning them. With sequential partitioning, balanced quicksort has work $\Theta(n\log n)$ and span $\Theta(n)$, so average parallelism is only $\Theta(\log n)$. An imbalanced pivot can make work and span quadratic. Random pivots or robust partitioning, a task-size cutoff and load balancing help. A work-efficient parallel partition reduces partition depth to $O(\log n)$; in a balanced recursion this gives $O(\log^2 n)$ span while retaining $O(n\log n)$ work.
AAPP-19-012: **Gather**, if the ten-element auxiliary array contains the input indices to read: `out[i]=input[index[i]]` for `i=0..9`, so output length is 10. A scatter normally supplies one destination index for each input value and therefore requires 100 such indices for 100 inputs. Merely knowing array sizes is insufficient without their roles, so the interpretation of the auxiliary array as an index list is essential.
AAPP-19-013: A separating hyperplane partitions an iteration/dependence space into ordered fronts so that required predecessors lie on earlier fronts, while operations on the same front are independent. For a 2D recurrence depending on the cell above and to the left, the anti-diagonals `i+j=k` are parallel fronts: compute increasing `k`, processing all cells on each front concurrently. A valid choice must orient every dependence forward; an arbitrary geometric cut is not necessarily a valid schedule.
AAPP-19-015:
Zip combines equally indexed elements of multiple collections into tuples; Unzip separates a tuple collection into component arrays:

```text
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1: tuples[i] = (a[i], b[i])  // zip
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:                         // unzip
    a[i] = tuples[i].first
    b[i] = tuples[i].second
```

Assume valid equal lengths (or a specified truncation policy), distinct destinations and no harmful aliasing. Both have $\Theta(n)$ work and $O(1)$ depth with $n$ processors under unit-cost tuple access. Zip may also denote elementwise processing of several aligned inputs, e.g. `c[i]=a[i]+b[i]`; state the chosen convention.

AAPP-19-035:
Shift moves elements by a fixed displacement. Define boundaries explicitly; for a non-cyclic right shift by $d\ge0$ with padding:

```text
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:
    out[i] = (i >= d) ? input[i-d] : pad
```

Use separate input/output storage so writes cannot destroy unread values. Work is $\Theta(n)$ and PRAM depth is $O(1)$ with $n$ processors; each valid input is read at most once, so EREW suffices. A cyclic shift instead uses `input[(i-d+n)%n]` after normalizing $d$ modulo $n$; it has the same costs.
AAPP-19-041: Fork-join creates/activates concurrent branches and later waits for their completion. A barrier is a rendezvous for an already existing group: each participant waits until all required participants arrive, then they can continue. A barrier does not itself create work or terminate threads; a join concerns completion of the joined branches/tasks. Fork-join implementations may use a barrier internally, but the abstractions describe different behavior.
AAPP-19-042: Map processes a fixed input collection, with one independent application per element. Workpile processes a dynamically managed set of tasks; workers can add more tasks, and the task count and costs may be irregular. Both can use a fixed worker pool, but workpile additionally needs a safe queue, load balancing and termination detection that accounts for active task generators.
AAPP-19-043: Compute each mapped value and immediately combine it into a thread-local accumulator, then reduce the local accumulators. For example, sum squares using `sum += x[i]*x[i]` with OpenMP `reduction(+:sum)`. This preserves linear work and logarithmic ideal reduction depth while removing the intermediate array, an extra memory pass and often a synchronization point. The reduction operator must permit the chosen reassociation, and the map must have no conflicting shared effects.
AAPP-19-046: A map function should be independent across elements. Shared mutable state can cause races, order-dependent results and contention; a lock may restore correctness while serializing the hot path. Use immutable shared inputs, per-iteration/per-thread state, or an explicit reduction for a shared aggregate. For example, updating a global pseudorandom generator from every map iteration is unsafe or contentious; use independent streams or an index-based generator.
AAPP-19-057:
Unsplit reverses a stable two-way Split when the original Boolean mask and the order of the two groups are retained. If group 1 occupies `[0,K)` and group 0 occupies `[K,n)`, then:

```text
s = exclusive_scan(mask, +, 0)
K = sum(mask)                       // also available from the scan
parallel for i = 0 .. n-1:
    src = mask[i] ? s[i] : K + (i - s[i])
    original[i] = split_array[src]
```

This is a scan followed by a gather; source positions are unique. Work is $\Theta(n)$ and depth is $\Theta(\log n)$ on a work-efficient EREW PRAM implementation. Without the mask or equivalent permutation metadata the original interleaving cannot generally be recovered.
AAPP-19-061: Map-Reduce first independently transforms inputs and then combines the results using an associative operator. A standard example is the sum of squares, $\sum_i x_i^2$, or the Monte Carlo $\pi$ computation in the bank: map each point to an inside-circle indicator and sum the indicators. Fuse transformation into each local reduction. For constant-cost transforms, work is $\Theta(n)$ and work-efficient PRAM depth is $\Theta(\log n)$; with $p$ processors, $O(n/p+\log p)$ time is achievable. These are standard examples; the supplied course notes do not identify which example was shown in this particular lecture.
AAPP-19-063: A Scan-Reduce pipeline computes all prefixes and then reduces those prefixes. For example, scan account changes to obtain balances $b_i=\sum_{j\le i}x_j$, then reduce with maximum to obtain the largest balance. A work-efficient scan and a tree reduction each use $\Theta(n)$ work and $\Theta(\log n)$ depth, so the composition has the same asymptotic bounds. If the requested result is merely the total sum of inputs, the final prefix already contains it and an additional reduction is unnecessary.
